source.title: Differentiating through the Fréchet Mean
source.authors: Aaron Lou; Isay Katsman; Qingxuan Jiang; Serge J. Belongie; Ser-Nam Lim; Christopher De Sa

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or corruption.
record.tranche_reason: Tests hyperbolic batch normalization on graph tasks, extending batch-normalization results to hyperbolic neural networks and different datasets.
record.gate_note: The paper reports faster convergence and better final validation loss and ROC AUC with hyperbolic batch normalization. Other BN results cited as motivation are prior work, not rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares two-layer hyperbolic neural networks with and without hyperbolic batch normalization. Its validation convergence results test V6's faster-learning component in a new setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record correctly summarizes the batch-normalization conclusion: the authors report faster validation convergence and better final validation loss and ROC AUC with hyperbolic batch normalization, paralleling benefits reported for Euclidean batch normalization.
record.recipe_differences: Uses hyperbolic batch normalization in two-layer hyperbolic encoders on graph link-prediction datasets; reports validation loss and ROC AUC rather than the version's stated Euclidean benchmarks.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset varies across CoRA, Disease, and Disease-M; authors say the improvement occurs regardless of dataset hyperbolicity.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed Fréchet mean solver converges faster than fixed-step Riemannian gradient descent and Karcher flow.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A specialized solver can accelerate hyperbolic Fréchet mean computation; this does not measure neural-network training effects in V1–V6.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing tangent-space aggregation with the Fréchet mean improves link-prediction performance on tree-like graphs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Geometrically faithful aggregation can improve hyperbolic graph-network predictive performance.

record.problems: The batch-normalization comparison is presented in plots without exact values in the text. The supplied description does not state uncertainty for these plots. The tasks are graph link prediction, not the classification benchmarks in the claim versions.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error in large convolutional networks, CIFAR datasets, random labels, and size or regularization effects.
Teacher-student ReLU networks, spurious local minima, and additional student neurons.
Depth-related training degradation, identity shortcuts, and deep plain or normalization-free residual networks.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, orthogonality, and trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss spikes, curvature dynamics, and divergence.
Higher-learning-rate tolerance, the named Euclidean architectures and datasets, and Fixup. The reported validation curves do not establish training-loss convergence or wall-clock speed.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text includes Figure 3's caption but no readable plotted values. Qualitative states rely on the authors' explicit descriptions. No learning-rate sweep, training-error comparison, or timing comparison for batch normalization is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, corrupted labels, model size, and the stated SGD/Adam recipes.
Teacher-student ReLU networks, spurious local minima, and student width.
Depth-related training error, identity shortcuts, and the stated special initialization or normalization-free residual recipes.
Initialization, signal and gradient propagation, and trainable depth.
Training dynamics around learning-rate stability limits and sharpness.
Tests hyperbolic batch normalization on two-layer hyperbolic neural network encoders for graph link prediction. Does not test Euclidean BN on MNIST, VGG/CIFAR-10, or Inception/ImageNet, nor Fixup.
